Admin Assist helps an administrator connect setup decisions with the evidence the system can inspect. Open it from the department menu. The page has setup wizard, setup report, explore ResGrid and add-ons, and an admin AI tab where that workspace is available. Our training stack has the setup tools while admin AI is disabled. We do not show an invented AI conversation. The nine-step wizard was covered earlier. In this lesson, we return after changing department
and dispatch settings, review the new findings, follow a link to the owning screen, and record a fresh review. Firehouse51 provides fictional data. A mobile response service, search department, security company, wildland contractor, or industrial emergency team can use the same administrative loop. Choose setup report. Current evidence shows 16 verified checks out of 25, nine needing attention, three critical and zero unknown.
Earlier recorded review remains 15 out of 23 with eight needing attention. Changed since review means configuration, selected scope, or the catalog has changed. Counts from different snapshots describe the checks in those snapshots. They are not a reliable department ranking. The new critical dispatch finding says shift coverage needs review. An empty shift can cause group dispatch to fall back to every group member. This appeared after we enabled shift dispatch in the previous lesson.
The setting is saved, but the coverage procedure still needs attention. For a security site, mobile response team, or volunteer search group, that fallback can reach a wider audience than the administrator intended. Verify again requests current evidence and refreshes the report time. It does not fix the findings. Review critical items first, then warnings and suggestions. Our report also shows administrator enrollment, recovery policy, notification preferences, communication verification
and empty group overlapping shifts and expiring qualifications. Follow each item to its responsible configuration screen and decide what operational review is needed. Suggestions are listed separately and are not counted as failures. Zero unknown means no listed check is currently unknown. It does not mean every department feature has been tested. The report explicitly lists apps and devices, deployments, and workforce and business operations as modules with no automated
checks yet. Those require their own review. A saved setup choice and a green module indicator cannot replace a device, provider, or workflow test. Explore ResGrid and add-ons, let an administrator search modules and features, including capabilities their menu or subscription may not show. Search for dispatch settings. The matching module explains why it matters, an example, prerequisites, key features, documentation, and owning screen links. Review the relevant feature.
We select that checkbox for dispatch settings. Back on the report, personal learning is one out of 62. Verified checks remain 16 out of 25 with nine needing attention. Learning progress records understanding by this user. It does not establish department setup, role eligibility, training competence, or readiness. Use the paid add-on filter to learn what requires separate access. Learning and interest choices do well.
Do not purchase an add-on, activate an external provider, import data, or send a message. From the dispatch settings feature, open-owning screen takes us to call and dispatch settings with a return banner. The banner says to save changes on this screen first, then return and verify. The return link does not save this form. Here, we inspect the already saved shift configuration, including its empty roster fallback, without making another change. Return to setup and verify takes us back
to setup report. For a search department, the next responsible review might inspect mobilization coverage. For mobile response, it might inspect the schedule team. For security or industry, site coverage. For a contractor, an extended assignment roster. Use the evidence link to investigate the actual problem, instead of changing several unrelated controls until the report appears better. After reviewing the listed findings, choose mark this report reviewed. The new administrative snapshot
records 16 out of 25, nine needing attention, and zero unknown. The live report still contains the three critical findings. Reviewed records that an administrator reviewed the report. It does not clear findings or certify operational readiness. Our existing follow-up date is October 16th. A review date is stored as a UTC calendar date and shown with the report. The downloadable calendar reminder can be imported by the administrator. It is not an automatic department.
document message. Open a fresh printable report when you need a current handover copy. Assign each unresolved issue to its responsible person using your department's procedure and keep the source evidence and agreed follow-up available to the next administrator. For community paramedicine and mental health response, review team coverage, operational communications, and credential follow-up with the service owner. For search and rescue, review volunteer mobilization, overlapping assignments, equipment, and map freshness.
For security companies, review site groups, patrol coverage, and supervisor access. For wildland contractors, review seasonal rosters, expiring qualifications, and extended deployments. For industrial emergency teams, review facility groups, equipment readiness, and continuity procedures. The check has value when someone investigates its operational consequence. Your practice exercise is to make a single authorized change in a training department, refresh the report,
explain any new finding, open its owning screen, verify what is saved, and record a review that preserves unresolved issues. Admin AI conversations, change plans, digests, and other unavailable workspace paths need separate configuration and verification. This recording proves only the setup, exploration, and review workflow shown.
